50.title: Nets on the right side (Luke 5:1–11)
50.hook: fishermen catch nothing all night, try once more, and the nets tear
50.howItsDone: Christians often call themselves disciples of Jesus, and many churches speak of discipleship as a lifelong apprenticeship through prayer, scripture, worship and service. The fish became one of the earliest Christian symbols.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty days in the wilderness: bread, spectacle, power, and three refusals. Your line was not by bread alone. What did you say no to? Day fifty. Fifty days on the path.

You know the feeling of working all night on something and having nothing to show for it. The report that won't come together. The baby who won't settle. Now picture a lake at dawn, the Sea of Galilee. Some fishermen are pulling their boats up on the shore, washing their nets. They've been out all night, which is when you fished that lake, and they caught nothing. Not one fish. They're tired, and they want to go home. Meanwhile a crowd is pressing in around a teacher on the beach, so many people he can hardly stand. He steps into one of the boats, the one that belongs to a fisherman named Simon, and asks him to push out a little. Today's word: disciple.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING TO SHOW.` → `EMPTY NETS AT DAWN.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO SIMON'S BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon, in the King James Bible: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the professional here. Jesus is a teacher from inland. And Simon's answer is honest and tired: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless. That one word is the hinge. He doesn't feel it. He does it anyway. And the net fills so full it starts to tear. They wave to their partners, James and John, in the other boat, and both boats fill until they start to sink. Simon falls at his knees: "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." And Jesus says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." And they pull the boats up on the shore, the story says, "they forsook all, and followed him." At the best catch of their lives, they leave it on the beach. So here's today's word. Disciple, in the Greek of the Gospels, is mathetes, and it means a learner, a student, an apprentice. The English comes from the Latin discipulus, from discere, to learn. A disciple isn't mainly a fan or a follower. It's someone who goes to school with a teacher, walking beside him, watching how he does things. The Gospels use the word for a wide circle of people, women and men, and from them Jesus chose twelve. Simon, the one who said nevertheless, will be called Peter. It all starts with one more try.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `NEVERTHELESS AT THY WORD.` · `THE NETS BREAK.` · `A DISCIPLE IS A LEARNER.` · then, large: `THEY FORSOOK ALL, AND FOLLOWED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of one thing you've tried and given up on. A conversation that went nowhere. A skill you dropped. A door you knocked on once. Something you toiled at all night, and took nothing. Bring it to mind without blaming yourself. Then ask: is there one more try in me? Just one. Not forever. Picture yourself letting down the net one more time. If you pray, you can say Simon's word: nevertheless. The bell holds the time.
Disciple. From the Latin for learner, and the Greek mathetes: a student who walks beside the teacher. Simon's first lesson was one more try.
Your line: put out into the deep. Today, try one thing one more time, the thing you'd given up on. Day fifty.

what it means: a learner who walks beside a teacher, and in this story it starts with one more try on an empty lake.

51.title: The tax collector's party (Matthew 9:9–13)
51.hook: Jesus calls Matthew from his booth and eats with his shady friends
51.howItsDone: Many churches keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, in September in the West and in November in the Orthodox calendar. Christians often point to this story when welcoming newcomers or sharing meals with people who are left out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, disciple: a learner, and fishermen who tried one more time and left full nets on the beach. Your line was put out into the deep. What did you try again? Day fifty-one.

Every town has someone people avoid sitting next to. Maybe he cheated people. Maybe he works for someone everyone resents. Maybe it's just his reputation. In Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake, there's a booth by the road where goods passing through get taxed. The man in the booth is named Matthew. He collects money for the rulers who answer to Rome, and people assume tax collectors take extra for themselves. The Gospel doesn't say whether he did. Jesus walks past, stops, and looks right at him. Today, the tax collector's party.
screen: `THE ONE NOBODY SITS NEXT TO.` → `A BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `JESUS STOPS.`

segments.voice: Two words, in the King James Bible: "Follow me. And he arose, and followed him." No speech. No conditions. Get up. And Matthew does. Then comes the party. Matthew opens his house for a meal, and the text says many publicans and sinners came and sat down with Jesus and his disciples. Publican is the old word for tax collector. Sinners here means people known for breaking the law, the ones good families kept at a distance. Some Pharisees see it. The Pharisees were serious, devout teachers who cared deeply about keeping God's law in everyday life, including who you ate with, because sharing a table meant sharing a life. So they ask the disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?" It's a real question, and Jesus gives a real answer: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. Then he quotes the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice." Go and learn what that means, he says. And he finishes: "for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Notice where the calling happens. Not in the temple. At a tax booth, and then at a dinner table. In Mark and Luke the man at the booth is called Levi, and Christian tradition has long said this Matthew is the one whose name is on the first Gospel, though scholars still discuss who wrote it. Either way, the Gospel that bears his name tells his calling in one sentence. He got up.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself breathe. Now think about your table, whatever that means for you: your lunch spot, your group chat, the people you text back first. Who's always there? Now think of someone who's never there. Someone outside your circle. A coworker who eats alone. A neighbor you've never really met. A relative people roll their eyes at. Picture sharing one ordinary meal with them. What would you talk about? If you pray, you can name that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The tax collector's party. Matthew gets up from his booth, and Jesus eats at a table full of people others kept away from.
Your line: he came for the sick. This week, share a meal or a coffee with someone outside your circle, even for ten minutes. Day fifty-one.

52.title: Water into wine (John 2:1–11)
52.hook: a wedding runs dry; Mary tells the servants to do whatever he says
52.howItsDone: Many churches read the wedding at Cana at weddings and in the weeks after Epiphany, and Catholics pray it as the second luminous mystery of the rosary. Many Christians see in it a blessing on marriage and on ordinary celebrations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tax collector's party, and a table full of people others kept away from. Your line was he came for the sick. Who's outside your circle? Today, another party. Day fifty-two.

A cake collapses. A band doesn't show. Weddings go wrong. Here's one in a village in Galilee, a place called Cana. Jesus is there with his first disciples, and his mother is there too. And in the middle of the feast, the wine runs out. Historians of the period say that would have embarrassed the hosts badly, since a wedding feast put a family's hospitality on display. John doesn't explain any of that. He says only that the wine ran short, and that the mother of Jesus spoke up. Today, water into wine.
screen: `A WEDDING GOING WRONG.` → `CANA, IN GALILEE.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: She goes to her son, and in the King James Bible she says just four words: "They have no wine." Not a request exactly. Just the need, laid in front of him. His answer sounds sharp to our ears: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." But woman wasn't rude in his language; it was a respectful way to address someone, and he'll call her the same thing from the cross. Then Mary does something unexpected. She doesn't argue. She turns to the servants and says: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Those are her last recorded words in John's Gospel. And, a small surprise, John never gives her name. She's always the mother of Jesus. There are six stone water jars standing there, the kind used for washing by the rules of purity, each holding, the King James says, two or three firkins. That's a lot of water. Fill them with water, he says. They fill them to the brim. Now draw some out and take it to the head of the feast. And it's wine. The man in charge doesn't know where it came from, and he calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff after people have had plenty, but "thou hast kept the good wine until now." The King James calls it the beginning of miracles, but John's Greek word is semeion, a sign: something that points past itself. This is the first. Christians read Mary's part in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see her here bringing people's needs to her son. Many Protestants dwell on how she points away from herself: do whatever he tells you.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SAITH UNTO YOU, DO IT.` · `SIX STONE JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `THE FIRST OF HIS SIGNS.` · then, large: `THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of a celebration coming up in your life, or one going on around you right now. A birthday, a new baby, a friend's small win, a wedding, a holiday meal. Now look at it the way Mary looked at the wedding. Where is the wine running low? Who's doing all the work? Who's quietly worried it won't be enough? Notice one place that needs a hand. If you pray, you can bring it to God in four words: they have no wine. The bell holds the time.
Water into wine. A village wedding saved, six jars filled to the brim, and the first sign in John's Gospel.
Your line: do whatever he tells you. Today, notice one celebration that needs help, and quietly be the one who helps. Day fifty-two.

53.title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–30)
53.hook: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has a long conversation with Jesus across an old divide
53.howItsDone: Many churches read the woman at the well during Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep a Sunday of the Samaritan Woman in the Easter season, honoring her as Saint Photini. Christians often read the story when speaking of baptism and of welcoming people across divides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, water into wine, and a mother who said do whatever he tells you. Where did a celebration need your help? Today, more water, and a very long talk. Day fifty-three.

A stranger on a train. A seatmate at a wedding. Sometimes the talk that goes somewhere real is with someone nobody planned to meet. This one happens at a well in Samaria, in the middle of the day. John says it was about the sixth hour: noon, the heat at its worst. Jesus is tired from walking, and he sits down on the edge of the well while his disciples go into town for food. A woman comes out with a jar to draw water. Alone. And he speaks to her. Today, the woman at the well.
screen: `A CONVERSATION YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.` → `NOON, AT THE WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES ALONE.`

segments.voice: He says, in the King James Bible: "Give me to drink." And she's startled: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." Jews and Samaritans shared ancestors and the books of Moses, but they had long been divided over where God should be worshiped: Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, right above this well. A Jewish teacher didn't usually ask a Samaritan woman for a drink. He answers: "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Here's the wordplay. Living water, in Greek and in everyday speech then, meant running water, fresh from a spring, instead of still water in a cistern. She hears the plain meaning: you don't even have a bucket. He means something deeper: water that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life." Then he tells her about her own life: five husbands, and now a man who isn't her husband. Some preachers have assumed she was a scandal, and that's why she came at noon. The text never says why. A woman then could be widowed, or sent away by a husband; John doesn't say what happened. What John does record is a long back-and-forth, about twenty verses of question and answer, and it's with her. She goes back to town, leaving her jar behind, and says: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Orthodox Christians remember her by the name Photini, the enlightened one.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `A JEW ASKS A SAMARITAN.` · `LIVING WATER MEANS RUNNING WATER.` · `SHE LEAVES HER JAR.` · then, large: `A WELL OF WATER SPRINGING UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one person you usually talk to only in passing. Quick hellos, quick texts, logistics. A parent, a coworker, a neighbor, someone who serves you coffee. Picture sitting down with them, no clock, no phone. What might you ask them that you never have? What might they tell you? Let that conversation play out in your mind for a moment. If you pray, you can ask for patience to listen. The bell holds the time.
The woman at the well. A Samaritan at noon, a Jewish teacher who asks her for a drink, and a long conversation across an old divide.
screen: `THE WOMAN AT THE WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: living water. Today, have one unhurried conversation. Put the phone away, ask a real question, and let it run. Day fifty-three.

54.title: A boy's lunch (John 6:1–14)
54.hook: five loaves and two fish from a child, and five thousand eat with baskets left over
54.howItsDone: Many churches read the feeding of the five thousand alongside teaching about communion and about sharing with people in need. Some church meals and food programs point to this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at the well, and a long talk at noon about living water. Did you have an unhurried conversation? Today, a hillside, and a hungry crowd. Day fifty-four.

Not enough money for the month. Not enough time for everything. Not enough patience for the kids tonight. Some sums never add up. Here's one on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out there, because they've seen him heal the sick. There are thousands of them, and nothing to eat. Jesus looks at the crowd, then turns to one of his disciples, Philip, and asks a question John says was a test: where are we going to buy bread for all these people? Today, a boy's lunch.
screen: `OBVIOUSLY NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HUNGRY CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `WHERE SHALL WE BUY BREAD?`

segments.voice: Philip does the math, in the King James Bible: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." A penny there is a denarius, a laborer's day's wage in one of Jesus's parables. So: two hundred days' wages wouldn't give everyone even a bite. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, comes back with something almost funny: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy. Barley, some readers point out, was the cheaper grain. This is a kid's packed lunch. And somebody has to hand it over. Jesus has the people sit down on the grass, about five thousand men, John says, and he takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Then comes a quieter line: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Twelve, from five loaves. Nothing wasted. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this feeding too; it's in all four Gospels. Christians read it as a wonder, and some also hear in it the table of communion, since he takes bread, gives thanks, and gives it. Later in the same chapter he calls himself the bread of life. But start with the boy. Nobody asks him to fix the problem. He just offers what he has, and it's small, and it's given away, and it turns out to be enough, with baskets to spare.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED DAYS' WAGES, NOT ENOUGH.` · `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `HE GIVES THANKS AND GIVES.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `THAT NOTHING BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of a need you know about right now. A friend who's struggling. A cause you care about. A tired colleague. A family member who's lonely. Now, instead of thinking about everything that would be needed, look at what you actually have. Maybe ten minutes. A skill. A spare meal. A kind word. Five loaves and two fish. Just notice it. Then picture handing it over. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first, the way he did. The bell holds the time.
A boy's lunch. Five barley loaves and two small fish, handed over on a hillside, and five thousand fed with twelve baskets to spare.
Your line: it was enough. Today, offer what you have, even if it's small, before you decide it doesn't count. Day fifty-four.

55.title: The storm (Luke 8:22–25)
55.hook: the boat is swamping, Jesus is asleep, and the disciples shout him awake
55.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear and illness, and it's often read at services for people at sea. The image of the church as a ship shows up in church architecture, in hymns, and in the name nave for the main hall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy's lunch: five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left over. Your line was it was enough. What did you offer? Today we're back on the lake, and the weather turns. Day fifty-five.

Think of three in the morning, when a worry gets loud. The bill, the diagnosis, the text you shouldn't have sent. Everything feels like it's going under, and everyone else seems to be asleep. Now picture a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus says, let's go over to the other side of the lake, and they push off. The lake sits low among hills, and storms can drop onto it fast. As they sail, Luke says, Jesus falls asleep. Then the wind comes down, the waves come over the side, and the boat starts filling with water. These are fishermen. They know this lake. And they're terrified. Today, the storm.
screen: `3AM, AND EVERYTHING'S GOING UNDER.` → `HE FALLS ASLEEP.` → `THE BOAT FILLS WITH WATER.`

segments.voice: They wake him, in the King James Bible, with a shout: "Master, master, we perish." In Mark's telling they're even more raw: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care? It's one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and it's shouted at a sleeping man in a sinking boat. And the text doesn't scold them for shouting. Then Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." Mark gives the words he speaks to the sea: "Peace, be still." He talks to the storm the way you'd calm a frightened animal. And then there's a silence so big that it frightens the disciples in a new way. Mark says they feared exceedingly. He turns to them: "Where is your faith?" And they whisper to each other: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." In the Hebrew scriptures, the one who stills the sea is God. One psalm says of sailors in a storm: "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." So that's the question the story leaves in the boat: who is this? Christians have long seen the church itself as a boat on rough water, and the main hall of many church buildings is still called the nave, from the Latin word for ship. And here's one more thing. Notice that he was in the boat the whole time. Asleep, but there. The story doesn't promise there'll be no storms. It puts him in the same wet boat as everyone else.
screen: `MASTER, CAREST THOU NOT?` · `HE REBUKED THE WIND.` · `WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?` · `THE NAVE: THE CHURCH AS A BOAT.` · then, large: `PEACE, BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and feel your feet on the floor. Now name the storm you're in. Not in general. Specifically. The one that keeps you up. Say it out loud, quietly, in one sentence, even if nobody hears. The disciples didn't dress it up. Then take three slow breaths, and on each out-breath let your shoulders drop a little. If you pray, you can shout it honestly, like they did, or say the words Peace, be still. If you don't, just let the breath be the calm. The bell holds the time.
The storm. A swamping boat, a sleeping teacher, a shout of don't you care, and a calm that frightened them all over again.
Your line: peace, be still. Today, when the storm gets loud, name it out loud once, and take one slow breath before you answer it. Day fifty-five.

56.title: Peter walks on water (Matthew 14:22–33)
56.hook: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and is caught by the hand
56.tomorrow: Who do you say I am?
56.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Peter's words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and the story is often preached on trust and doubt. Icons and paintings of the scene show Christ's hand reaching for Peter as he sinks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the storm: a sleeping teacher, a shout, and peace, be still. What storm did you name? Today closes week eight, and the road through Galilee. One more night on the lake. Day fifty-six.

The first day of a new job. Asking someone out. Standing up to speak. There's a moment where a person either steps out or doesn't. Back to the lake, the same night as the boy's lunch. Jesus sends the disciples ahead in the boat and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Out on the water the wind is against them, and the waves toss the boat. Then, Matthew says, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see him coming toward them, walking on the sea. They scream. They think it's a ghost. Today, Peter walks on water.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE YOU STEP OUT.` → `THE FOURTH WATCH OF THE NIGHT.` → `A FIGURE WALKING ON THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Straightaway he speaks, in the King James Bible: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." And Peter, of course it's Peter, answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: come. And Peter climbs over the side. He actually walks. Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me." That's the whole shape of the story. He steps out. He looks at the wind instead of the one he's walking toward. He sinks. A prayer of three words: Lord, save me. No time for more. And then: "And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Immediately. Not after a lesson. The hand comes first, and the question after. Little faith, in Matthew's Greek, is one word, oligopistos. It's almost a nickname. Matthew's Jesus uses it for his disciples more than once. Little faith. Not no faith. Enough to step out, not quite enough to keep looking up. And when they climb back in, the wind stops, and the people in the boat worship him and say, of a truth thou art the Son of God. That's where these two weeks on the road through Galilee end. Stargazers, a family fleeing, a boy asking questions, a wild man, a river, a desert, full nets, a party, a wedding, a well, a lunch, a storm. And now a man sinking, and a hand.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER; IT IS I.` · `BID ME COME UNTO THEE.` · `HE SAW THE WIND, AND SANK.` · `LITTLE FAITH, NOT NO FAITH.` · then, large: `LORD, SAVE ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and feel your weight in the chair. Think of one step you've been waiting to feel ready for. A call, an application, an apology, a hard conversation, a first try at something. Picture yourself taking it. Not the whole journey, just the first step over the side. Notice where your eyes go. To the wind? To what could go wrong? Then remember the hand in the story, which came immediately. If you pray, you can use Peter's three words. The bell holds the time.
